cues.text: It is Friday.
Last week, Ken decided to play volleyball with his team on Saturday.
At school, Mia asks him about tomorrow.
Ken says: I'm going to play volleyball.
The plan was in his head before Mia asked.
We use be going to for a plan.
A plan is something we want to do and have already decided.
The important idea is time: we made the plan before we speak.
Ken did not decide when Mia asked.
He decided last week.
The form has three pieces.
First comes am, is or are.
Then come going to and a base verb.
A base verb is the simple verb, like play, watch or buy.
It has no -s, -ed or -ing.
For a question, put am, is or are before the person.
For a negative, put not after am, is or are.
In speaking we usually say the short forms I'm, he's, we're, isn't and aren't.

Here are five examples:

I'm going to play volleyball on Saturday.
Ken made this plan last week.
My sister is going to visit our grandmother tomorrow.
She called her yesterday.
We're going to watch a film tonight.
We already have the tickets.
Are you going to come to the game?
Mia wants to know Ken's plan.
Ken isn't going to study this weekend.
He is going to play games at home.
A common mistake is to forget am, is or are.
I going to play is wrong.
I am going to play is right.
Another mistake is to change the verb after going to.
He is going to plays is wrong, because a base verb never takes -s.
On Saturday, Ken arrives at the game and says: Oh no, I forgot my water!
Mia answers: I'll give you some of mine.
Mia did not plan this.
She decided at that moment, when she heard the problem.
We use will in three common situations.
First, a decision we make now, while we speak.
Second, an offer, when we say we can do something for another person.
Third, a promise, when we tell someone we will really do something.
The form is will and a base verb.
It is the same for every person: I will, she will, they will.
Never add -s or to after will.
She will help is right.
She will helps and she will to help are wrong.
The negative is will not, usually said won't.
For a question, put will before the person.
The short answers are Yes, I will and No, I won't.

Here are five examples:

The phone is ringing.
I'll answer it.
This is a decision now.
Your bag looks heavy.
I'll carry it for you.
This is an offer.
I'll call you after the game.
This is a promise.
Will you help me with my homework?
This is a question.
Don't worry.
I won't tell anyone.
This is a promise with the negative.
Notice and compare these two short talks.
In both, Mia says: We need more balls for practice.
Ken: I know.
I'm going to bring two from home.
Ken: Oh, OK.
I'll bring two from home.
Both sentences are correct.
In the first, Ken already had the plan.
In the second, he decides when Mia speaks.
Which words show the difference?
Predictions are different.
A prediction is what we think will happen.
Here both forms are often correct.
Our team will win and our team is going to win can both be right.
But we may see a sign now, like dark clouds.
Then people often choose going to: Look at those clouds.
It's going to rain.
In speaking and in messages to friends, we usually use short forms.
When we write a short form, an apostrophe shows where letters are missing.
An apostrophe is a small mark at the top of the letters.
It looks like a comma.
I will becomes I'll.
The apostrophe takes the place of the letters wi.
We will becomes we'll.
You'll, he'll, she'll and they'll work in the same way.
Will not becomes won't.
This one is special.
We do not write willn't.
Will changes to wo, and not changes to n't.
The apostrophe takes the place of the o in not.

Here are four examples:

I'll see you on Saturday.
We'll bring the ball.
I won't be late.
They'll wait for us at the door.
The apostrophe matters.
Without it, we'll becomes well, and I'll becomes ill.
These are different words.
You feel well when you are OK.
You feel ill when you are sick.
Also, a short answer with yes uses the long form.
Say Yes, I will, not Yes, I'll.
